concept.name: Split-Brain Prevention

relationships.description: Connects Split-Brain Prevention to caching in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Split-brain happens when a network partition splits a distributed cluster into isolated groups that both elect a primary and accept conflicting writes; preventing it requires strict majority quorums (N/2 + 1), time-bounded leases, and monotonic fencing tokens.
spark.keyTakeaway: Never rely on heartbeats alone to declare a peer dead—pair majority quorum (odd node count >= 3) with monotonic fencing tokens checked by the storage layer so a paused old primary can never corrupt data.

concept.whyItMatters: A single 15-second split-brain event in a primary-replica database or distributed lock service allows two leaders to commit conflicting transactions (e.g., double-spending balances or diverging PostgreSQL LSNs), requiring painful manual data reconciliation or full cluster rebuilds.
whenToUse: Operating stateful primary-replica databases (PostgreSQL via Patroni, MySQL Group Replication) with automated failover.
Building distributed lock managers, leader-elected controllers, or consensus stores (etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul, Raft).
Managing shared block/object storage (Ceph, DRBD, Pacemaker) where two writers would corrupt filesystem metadata.
whenNotToUse: Stateless, idempotent microservices behind a load balancer where any instance can serve requests independently.
AP/eventual-consistency stores (e.g., Cassandra, DynamoDB multi-master with CRDTs or LWW) intentionally designed to accept concurrent writes and merge them later.
Single-node deployments where no automated failover exists (manual promotion avoids accidental dual-primary).
keyPoints: Majority Quorum (`floor(N / 2) + 1`) guarantees any two quorums overlap in at least one node—3 nodes tolerate 1 failure, 5 nodes tolerate 2.
A 2-node cluster cannot form a safe majority quorum (half of 2 is 1); always deploy 3 nodes or add a lightweight Witness/Arbitrator in a 3rd failure domain.
Leases alone are vulnerable to asymmetric clock drift or long JVM/hypervisor pauses (a 20s GC pause outlives a 10s lease, leaving the old leader thinking it still holds the lock).
Fencing tokens (monotonically increasing epoch/term numbers issued by the consensus store) must be validated by the storage/target server to reject stale writes.
STONITH (Shoot The Other Node In The Head) uses out-of-band power/hypervisor APIs (IPMI, AWS EC2 StopInstances) to guarantee an unreachable node is truly dead before failover.

examples.title: Fencing Tokens Stopping a GC-Paused Leader
examples.scenario: Service Node A acquires a distributed lease (`epoch=33`) in etcd to write to an object store, then freezes for 25 seconds during a JVM Stop-The-World GC pause. etcd expires the lease at 10s and grants `epoch=34` to Node B.
examples.outcome: When Node A wakes up and sends its buffered write tagged with `epoch=33`, the storage server sees `last_seen_epoch=34` and rejects Node A's stale request with `412 Precondition Failed`.

examples.title: PostgreSQL + Patroni 3-Node Quorum Failover
examples.scenario: A primary PostgreSQL node in AZ-1 loses network connectivity to AZ-2 and AZ-3 while remaining reachable by a few local app servers.
examples.outcome: Because AZ-1 holds only 1 of 3 etcd votes, Patroni in AZ-1 fails to renew its leader key, immediately demotes local Postgres to read-only (`pg_rewind` on rejoin), while AZ-2/AZ-3 form a 2/3 quorum and promote the replica cleanly.

tradeOffs.pro: Strict majority quorum guarantees zero split-brain writes during any network partition.
tradeOffs.con: If >= `ceil(N / 2)` nodes are unreachable (e.g., 2 of 3 nodes down), the entire cluster stops accepting writes until quorum returns.

tradeOffs.pro: 5 nodes survive 2 simultaneous failures (e.g., 1 planned maintenance + 1 sudden crash) without losing quorum.
tradeOffs.con: Increases write commit latency (must replicate to 3 nodes instead of 2) and adds 67% more infrastructure cost.

tradeOffs.factor: Fencing Tokens vs. STONITH Hardware Fencing
tradeOffs.pro: Fencing tokens work purely in software over standard protocols (HTTP `If-Match`, Raft term checks) with zero hardware dependencies.
tradeOffs.con: Requires the downstream resource to understand and enforce monotonic tokens; legacy filesystems/SANs often require STONITH power-off instead.

failureModes.name: Even-Node Cluster Without Witness
failureModes.description: A 2-node active-passive pair splits down the middle; if each side promotes itself on heartbeat loss, both accept writes.
failureModes.mitigation: Always use an odd number of voting members (3 or 5) or place a lightweight quorum witness in a 3rd AZ/region.

failureModes.name: Asymmetric Partition / Zombie Leader
failureModes.description: Old leader loses contact with peers but stays reachable by clients, continuing to serve stale reads or attempt writes before its lease expires.
failureModes.mitigation: Use ReadIndex / leader leases in Raft for linearizable reads, demote immediately on failed lease renewal, and enforce fencing tokens on all writes.

failureModes.name: Hypervisor Pause / Clock Jump
failureModes.description: A VM live-migration or NTP step causes a node's wall clock to lag or jump, breaking lease-expiry assumptions.
failureModes.mitigation: Use monotonic clocks (`CLOCK_MONOTONIC`) for lease intervals, keep conservative safety margins, and rely on storage-side fencing tokens rather than timing alone.

failureModes.name: Dual-STONITH Shootout
failureModes.description: Two partitioned nodes simultaneously send IPMI/cloud-API power-off commands to each other, taking down the entire cluster.
failureModes.mitigation: Gate STONITH behind quorum checks, or configure asymmetric fencing delays (e.g., Node 1 waits 0s, Node 2 waits 5s).

commonMistakes: Deploying a 2-node cluster with automated failover and no 3rd-AZ witness.
Using `wall-clock` (`CLOCK_REALTIME`) instead of monotonic clocks (`CLOCK_MONOTONIC`) to measure lease expiration.
Assuming a distributed lock (like Redis Redlock without fencing) prevents stale writes after a client process pauses.
Placing 2 of 3 consensus nodes in the same availability zone or rack—losing that single AZ loses quorum.
Rejoining a fenced old primary without `pg_rewind` or log truncation, causing silent replication corruption.

sections.content:
## The idea

**Split-brain** occurs when a network partition divides a cluster into two or more isolated sub-networks and more than one side believes it is the active authority. In a stateful system, two concurrent primaries inevitably generate **divergent histories** that cannot be merged automatically.

Preventing split-brain rests on three interlocking guarantees:

1. **Mathematical Quorum (`floor(N / 2) + 1`):** Only a partition containing a strict majority of voting nodes may elect a leader or commit writes. By the pigeonhole principle, two majorities always share at least one overlapping node.
2. **Time-Bounded Leases & Demotion:** A leader holds a renewable lease (e.g., `10s` TTL in etcd/Consul) and must demote itself to read-only the instant renewal fails—before any peer can safely take over.
3. **Storage-Side Fencing:** Because process pauses (GC, swap, VM migration) can freeze a leader past its lease expiry, the storage or target system must enforce a **monotonic fencing token** (or hardware STONITH) so late packets from a zombie leader are rejected.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a **3-AZ Patroni + etcd PostgreSQL failover** combined with **storage-level fencing** during a partition:

1. **Steady state:** `Node-A` (AZ-1) holds etcd leader lease `term=42` (`ttl=10s`, `loop_wait=2s`). `Node-B` (AZ-2) and `Node-C` (AZ-3) stream WAL replication.
2. **Network partition (`t = 0s`):** AZ-1 is cut off from AZ-2 and AZ-3. `Node-A` can still talk to a few AZ-1 app pods, so it thinks it is healthy.
3. **Self-demotion (`t = 2s–6s`):** `Node-A` attempts to renew its `term=42` lease in etcd, but cannot reach `Node-B` or `Node-C` (1/3 votes < quorum of 2). Before its `10s` TTL expires, Patroni on `Node-A` **forcibly demotes local PostgreSQL to read-only**.
4. **Quorum election (`t = 10s`):** `Node-B` and `Node-C` form a 2/3 majority in etcd, expire `term=42`, and elect `Node-B` as primary with **`term=43`**.
5. **Zombie protection:** Even if `Node-A` had frozen in a 20-second kernel/GC stall before demoting and later flushed a write tagged `epoch=42` to a shared volume or conditional store, the store sees `current_epoch=43 > 42` and **rejects the write**. When AZ-1 heals, `Node-A` runs `pg_rewind` to discard any uncommitted local WAL and rejoins as a replica.

sections.content:
## Quorum math and failure-domain placement

Consensus protocols (Raft, Paxos, ZAB) require `Q = floor(N / 2) + 1` votes:

- **N = 3:** Quorum = 2, fault tolerance = **1 node**. Place 1 node in each of 3 AZs (`1 + 1 + 1`). Never place `2 + 1` across 2 AZs—if the 2-node AZ goes down, quorum is lost.
- **N = 5:** Quorum = 3, fault tolerance = **2 nodes**. Ideal for production etcd/ZooKeeper where one node can be down for OS patching while still surviving a sudden crash.
- **Even N (2 or 4):** Adds zero fault tolerance over `N - 1` (`4` nodes still have quorum `3`, tolerating only `1` failure) while increasing replication overhead. If you only have 2 database servers, run a tiny **quorum witness** in a 3rd AZ/region.

## Split-brain prevention mechanisms compared

| Mechanism | How It Stops Split-Brain | Guarantees Against GC/Clock Pause? | Typical Systems |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Majority Quorum (Raft/Paxos)** | Only `> N/2` partition can elect a leader | Yes (for consensus state) | etcd, Consul, ZooKeeper, CockroachDB |
| **Monotonic Fencing Tokens** | Target storage rejects writes with `token < max_seen` | **Yes** (enforced at write time) | HDFS NameNode, Chubby, S3/DynamoDB conditional writes |
| **STONITH / Power Fencing** | Cuts power/network to unreachable node via IPMI/Cloud API | **Yes** (node is physically halted) | Pacemaker/Corosync, Linux DRBD, Ceph |
| **TTL Leases Alone** | Leader steps down if lease isn't renewed in `T` seconds | **No** (vulnerable to pauses `> T`) | Naive Redis locks, un-fenced leader election |

## Failure modes

- **Silent Stale Reads from Zombie Leader:** Even if writes are fenced, an isolated old primary can still serve stale reads to clients unless reads also go through quorum (`ReadIndex`) or use bounded leader leases with monotonic clocks.
- **Split-Brain in Async Replicas:** Promoting an asynchronous PostgreSQL/MySQL replica before draining the old primary loses committed transactions on the old primary that hadn't replicated yet (**RPO > 0**), causing diverged timelines.
- **Witness Co-Location:** Running the 3rd-vote witness on the same physical host or VPC subnet as Node 1 turns a 3-node cluster into a single-point-of-failure 2-node cluster in disguise.
- **Fencing Token Wrap or Non-Persistence:** If the storage node resets `max_seen_epoch` to `0` on reboot, a stale zombie packet can slip through after a restart.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / Lightweight fencing with cloud conditional writes
sections.content:
## Lightweight fencing with cloud conditional writes

You don't always need a dedicated etcd cluster to get strong fencing. Modern cloud object and NoSQL stores provide atomic **compare-and-swap (CAS)** primitives:

- **Amazon S3 / GCS:** Use `If-Match: <ETag>` or `If-None-Match: *` on lease/manifest objects so only the holder of the latest ETag can commit a checkpoint.
- **DynamoDB:** Use `ConditionExpression: "epoch = :expected"` to increment a monotonic `epoch` attribute and attach that `epoch` to every downstream mutation.
- **Kubernetes Leases:** `coordination.k8s.io/v1` `Lease` objects use optimistic concurrency (`resourceVersion`) inside Kubernetes' etcd-backed API server.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Deploy an **odd number** of consensus/voting nodes (3 or 5) distributed across **>= 3 independent failure domains** (AZs).
- [ ] Never run a 2-node active-passive cluster with auto-failover without a 3rd-AZ witness.
- [ ] Pair leader leases with **monotonic fencing tokens** validated by the downstream storage/database.
- [ ] Configure STONITH (IPMI or Cloud Stop-Instance) for shared-disk/block clusters where software fencing isn't possible.
- [ ] Use monotonic clocks (`CLOCK_MONOTONIC`) for all lease-expiry timers.
- [ ] Chaos-test network partitions (e.g., `iptables DROP` between AZs) and `SIGSTOP` pauses on the leader to verify zero dual-primary writes.

nodes.label: Consensus Store (etcd/Raft)
nodes.role: 3-node quorum across 3 AZs; issues monotonic ter

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Split-brain happens when a network partition splits a distributed cluster into isolated groups that both elect a primary and accept conflicting writes; preventing it requires strict majority quorums (N/2 + 1), time-bounded leases, and monotonic fencing tokens.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: New Leader (Node B) applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Fenced Storage / Target.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Fenced Storage / Target experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Always use an odd number of voting members (3 or 5) or place a lightweight quorum witness in a 3rd AZ/region.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Never rely on heartbeats alone to declare a peer dead—pair majority quorum (odd node count >= 3) with monotonic fencing tokens checked by the storage layer so a paused old primary can never corrupt data.
Avoid trap: Deploying a 2-node cluster with automated failover and no 3rd-AZ witness.
Avoid trap: Using `wall-clock` (`CLOCK_REALTIME`) instead of monotonic clocks (`CLOCK_MONOTONIC`) to measure lease expiration.
When to reach for it: Operating stateful primary-replica databases (PostgreSQL via Patroni, MySQL Group Replication) with automated failover.
When to reach for it: Building distributed lock managers, leader-elected controllers, or consensus stores (etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul, Raft).

putItTogether.title: Putting Split Brain Prevention Together
putItTogether.summary: Never rely on heartbeats alone to declare a peer dead—pair majority quorum (odd node count >= 3) with monotonic fencing tokens checked by the storage layer so a paused old primary can never corrupt data.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Split Brain Prevention before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: When Node A wakes up and sends its buffered write tagged with `epoch=33`, the storage server sees `last_seen_epoch=34` and rejects Node A's stale request with `412 Precondition Failed`.
